No news of the week seems to have loather 0 bid &MakOad a I e • tenet than A, eter in the announcement that a new gold Sold has brim discovered. This latest Eldorado is Situated in the Far -the very Far—North of Ameri.. The Yoko° district in which the gold- bearing play, 1.4 11,0 Wen Cereal is only a portion, and bitl,ort ii very insignificant portion,of Canada yet in extent it is air rut the IliZa of France. It is bounded on the south hy British (Voluble, on the sweet by the UMW,' Stator territory of Alaska, on the east by the Rocky Mountains and on the north by the Arctic Ocean. It appears to be a wild and inhospitable region and is closed by ice and snow for a considerable pert of the year. Yet, the fact that gold hoe been found in large quantities has already ceased • " rosli "of !ninon, from various parts of the United Staten and Canada. There appears to be now no doinit about the richness of this gold-field. It has hem partially worked by a few prospectors for alm.t twenty years, and tee Lieutenant' Governor of the North-W.terri Provinces state that the yield gold last winter was of the wine of about three million &Mara. Inspector Coarrornuit,of the North-Went Molintad reports to his Government that" there is hardly a creek within 300 indes sous h-w.t or north-east in which more or less gold is not found." The true value of the mineral wealth of this part of the country will, he adds, not be known for many years to COMP es new diacoverion are being made each seaeon. The latest reports from what is known as the Klondike region are of a parti- milady attractive d.cliption. It is said that one fortunate miner s.urei gold worth six hundred dollar; from three " pans " of earth. Another account nays, "Those who cannot get claims are buying in on those already located. Men cannot be got to work for love or money. One and a half dollars per hour is the wage paid the few men who hire for work, and work as many hours as yon like. , Some of the claims are no rich that every night a I few pans of dirt suffice to pay the hired help, when there is any:' It is not surprising when ap- parently authentic reports of this dercription are circulated, that the "gold fever "bas broken out with unbounded virulence.

Mr. T, J. Down the manager and secretary to Messes. greened!, Whitley,and Co.gave some rather remarkable evidence bet.ire the Boys; Commission on the Licensing Laws last week. In its effect, Mr.Down's evidence can nattily be deriribed &neither more or less than a direct charge of politi- cal bias against the Warrington bench in its deal- ings with licensing casee. He said, ac,tording to the newspaper reports, that there are in Warring- ton ° magietrates who had in public apeechee denounced the liquor trade, and who were so biassed by their political and teetotal opinions ante be incapable of dealing with the question ;" andoigain, in answer to a question be said, "We have had cases w here licenses ,ere refused, and I think political feeling had something to do with it." Now, it would be interesting to know definitely what ° political opinions "or "political feelings" incapacitate a magistrate from acting judicially in licensing cases, in the opinion of the representatives of the brewers. Is every Liberal magistrate incapable of acting judicially in these I cases ? Because, after all, most Liberals hold the opinion very strongly that a good deal of reform is needed in connection with the liquor trade. Pro- posals which do not err on the side of modesty are occasionally made on behalf of brewing monopol- ists, bat a demand that no magistrate with a Libe- ral "bias" should deal with licensing cases would beat everything that has yet been heard of.

But the" is another side to this question of poli- tical bins. If there can be bias on the Warrington or any other bench against the bre were, there can also be bias in favour of them. It would be in- teresting to inquire which is the bias that prevails in Warrington. We are under the impreesion that Meesrs.Greenall. Whitley, and Co., for instance, have obtained all or nearly all the licenses they have asked for in this town. They may not always have got them at the Bret time of asking, but they have got them in the end. Within the last few years this firm has obtained a license for the new house in Battersby-lane and another for a house in Bewsey. If we may judge by the competition there was for them, these licenses are very valuable properties indeed. Mr. Bolton, wee, we believe, in the field before Messrs. Greenall, W hitley, and Com- pany for a license in Battersby-lane district,and the proprietors ot the " Grove " foes license in Bewaey, yet the licenses were uot granted to either of these applicante but to Messrs. Greenall. Whitley and Co. Now that the subject of magisterial bias hal been raised, it may be fairly asked, was there no bias on the Warrington bench when these licenses were granted ? It was certainly not the kind of bias of which Mr. Down complain., but it may have been a bias for sll that.

Another grievance against the local bench which Mr. Down 14,4 before the Royal Commission was that .4 special whip "is sent round to the magis- trates when serious canes under the licensing laws are down foe consideration—in other words that these cases are tried by the whole bench instead of by the small proportion of magistrates who gener- ally attend on any particular day. It is hani to see why this system should be complained about. It

seems to be an excellent device for guarding against the very bias that has been referred to. A small I bench of two or three or four magistrates might ! possibly be entirely composed of justices bimsed one way or the other, awl the eons. mooing of the whole of the magistrates was, one might think, just the precau- tion necessary to guard against this. The present system was adopted in 1892 upon a proposal by hir '. Monks, who ia about the last man en the bench to be accused of allowing a political bias te influ- ence his judicial decisions. Before 1892 there may have been a bias on the bench, but it was not gaMet the brewers. Publicans were occasionally sum mooed be breaches of licensing laws, but the cases were nearly always dismissed. In fact, when everything is taken into account it ia a trifle surprisinz to hear the Warrington flinch, of all benches, accused of bias against the liquor interest.

Turning to another iTaTt—of—Mr. Down'A evidence, it is astonishing to lind him defending the custom ; of sending children for beer. We were of opin- ion that this cantons was con demned'hy almost every body. The Chief Constable of Cheehire bail con- damned it in a circular to publicane, and it has , been condemned by the justices of Bootle and , Birkenhead, by the standing Joist Committee of

the County of Durham and other public auttiontise. It is erldent that the present rory Home Secretary in en' of Mr. D0W11.4 way of thinking on this sob- :lre% for in &wrier to a question in the Weise of Commons yesterday it was stated that he thought the example set by the Standing Joint Committee referred to was worthy of being followed.

Mr. S. Ellis,secretar; of Meows. P. Walker and Sons. Limit-d, also gave evidence before the Royal Commission. His evidence was mainly a ,lefence of the manager system of conducting public • houses, but we notice that some amusement was caused by. nuestion referring to an illustration in the book issued by Messrs. Walker which we no- ticed last week. This picture represents three monk, engaged in brewing ale and • fourth monk with the scriptures open before him at Rebrews XXX. Now as there only thirteen charmers in llebrewa what is the inner meaning of, this pic- ture ? fo it only • " goat," or is it meant to be syrobalical—eymbolical, that is, of a connection between the Church and the brewery? From the answer that was made before the Royal Commission it would seem that this is only a way of nlvertising the XXX. quality of beer or stout— on the whole • rather doubtful method of adver- tising beer.

John .doston.who appeared at Wa&ngton Police Court lust week to answer a charge of s'..•sling herbs from the garden of Councillor Heaton, is certainly a lucky Port of thief. When the case war tried it seemed likely to go hard with him, but Co ancillor Il.ston, the injured party, casually admit te I being the prisoner's uncle, which appeared to be some- thing in the tatter's favour. Alderman Stitt en only fined prisoner ss.,and than his generous and forgiv- ing uncle considerately paid the fine. Priaoner'e gratitude did not detain him in Court long, but his luck bad not left him, for the next minute he was to be seen shouldering the proceeds of his larceny and walking of with them without let or hind- rance.We ahould think that oaths whole,Councillor Heaton would have been better pleased had the depredator not got into the hands of the police. It would have saved him Sr. some inconvenience, and the herbs would have Mill remained in their pres- ent ownership. Such is justice however, and John Heaton paid the penalty of his crime in the eye of the law.

Mr. Seddon said refer- ence had berm made to the trade of the colonies, and the necessity for an improvement in trade with the mother country. He was one of these who thought it essential in the best interests of the Hidsli people and of the colonies that they should have more trade and keep eloper together. What had canoed him much thought had been the fact tout in the progress of trade with the colonies foreign nations had been steadily increasing, while there had been comparatively small perigee. in connection with the mother country. There ought to have been four times as much expansion. British trade An there had been. He wee not one of those who ho. Resod that the principal object of the colonies was to make room for the surplus population of the mother country. It wan never intended by nature that their youths should have to leave home to make a liv- ing. He pro- tested strongly aged.nt the negl•ct shown by the Press of England with regard to colonial affairs. STRIKE OF FUSTIAN CUTTERS AT WARRINOTON.

Qnite unexpectelly,the girls employed by Mews J. Platt and Son, fustian cutters, Warrington, came out on etrike on Wednesday last week. Work was begun se usual before breakfast but at eight o'clock the employee. at the levtlignenelsne shop met to- gether and the remit of their deliberations was a determination to strike. The was carried oat forth- with, and instead of returning to work they assembled in front of the firma offices in Lythgoes- ' lane, and indulged in booing and ahouting for some considerable time. On the doors and walls of the Lythgoes-lane ehop,which in the principal establieb- meet of the firm,coull he iseen.written in chalk each sentences an "Strike. Don't go in till you get a I rise,"" Rogers patent's ruined cutting," and "Strike of Cetera?' The girls afterwards marched to the other shops of the firm located in differentparts of the town, and induced them to Join in the strike. This they did, and Joined in proceesion through the streetn waving their shawls and singing snatches of i songs. By noon. 700 employes had struck work, and the establishments had to be closed for the day. The causes of the strike are not very clear. It ap- pears that on the 24th of [act month, the wages of a number of girls —about one in twenty of those employed were reduced to the extent of sixpence per week, and I although no complaints were made M the em- ployers, the reduction seems to have mimed irrita- tion amongst the workpeople. The chief cause of the dispute, however, appears to be the intoduction of &machine for foatian cutting, which will, in course of time, relent+ the number of hands re- quired. The machine is the patent of Mr. George I Roger, of Ellesmere-street, Warrington. Be it, ilinstead of the girl having to run along the aide of I the material whoa coiling /toily now merely stands at one end, and by turning a small wheel is enabled to send the cutting instrument from one end of the cloth to the other, end it afterwards returns to her. Megrim. Platt have the exclueive right in Warrington to work theme machines, which, se noon as they can be made, will be used on all the frames in their etitabliehments. .

It wee thought that tile girls would return to work on Thureday runrning.but they declined to do so, Mr. Platt arrived at the works at eleven o'clock, from Islandudno.and had a conference with the em- ployes! in one of the large room., interviewing about • dneen at a time. It appears that a desire for further remuneration was expreseed. Even- tually Mr. Platt, who showed every disposition to meet the hands generously, and much regrets the temporary strike, decided to grant certain small coneessione,which were accepted as perfectly fiStifl- factory to those to whom they were explained, but the majority of the other, do not appear to be die- posed at present to agree to them. On Friday, very few pereons had returned to work, and alihnugh the excitement ham greatly Rub- sided, there seeing very little diaposition on the part cot the employee' to return to their work.
